topic.title: Greedy & Intervals
topic.summary: Make the locally best choice and never look back — when you can prove it is safe. Merging, inserting and scheduling intervals, meeting rooms, reachability, and knowing when greedy fails and DP is needed.
topic.overview:
A **greedy algorithm** builds the answer one step at a time, always taking the choice that looks best right now (earliest finish, farthest reach, largest coin) and **never undoing it**. When it is correct it is usually the simplest and fastest solution: *sort + one pass*, O(n log n).

The catch: greedy is only correct when the problem has the **greedy-choice property** — some optimal solution starts with the greedy choice. Interviewers want you to either **justify** the choice (exchange argument) or **break** it with a small counter-example and switch to dynamic programming.

### Interval problems — the most common greedy family
Almost every interval question starts with **sorting**, and the sort key is the whole trick:
| Goal | Sort by | Then |
|---|---|---|
| Merge overlapping intervals | start | extend the last block or start a new one |
| Insert into a sorted list | (already sorted) | before / overlap / after in one pass |
| Keep the most non-overlapping intervals (min removals) | **end** | keep if start ≥ last kept end |
| Minimum rooms / max concurrency | start | min-heap of end times (or sorted starts + ends) |

**Overlap test** for `[a, b]` and `[c, d]`: they overlap when `a ≤ d && c ≤ b` (use `<` if touching should not count). Always ask whether touching intervals overlap.

### Other greedy patterns here
- **Farthest reach** (Jump Game): reachable positions form a prefix — track one number.
- **Reset on negative** (Gas Station): when a running sum drops below zero, no start in that stretch can work.
- **Last occurrence** (Partition Labels): extend the current block to the last copy of every character seen.

### What interviewers listen for
- Why the greedy choice is safe (one sentence of exchange argument), or a counter-example when it is not.
- The correct sort key and the exact comparison (`<` vs `≤`).
- Complexity: sorting dominates → O(n log n); the sweep itself is O(n).

questions.title: Merge Intervals
questions.prompt:
You are given a list of intervals `[start, end]` (in any order). Merge every group of **overlapping** intervals and return the resulting non-overlapping intervals sorted by start.

Intervals that only **touch** (`[1, 4]` and `[4, 5]`) count as overlapping and are merged.
hints: If the intervals were sorted by start, where could an interval that overlaps the current one be?
After sorting by start, each interval either overlaps the last merged block or starts after it — there is no third case.
Sort by start; keep a result list; if start ≤ last.end extend last.end = max(last.end, end), else push a new block.

approaches.name: Repeated pairwise merging
approaches.idea: Keep merging any two overlapping intervals until nothing changes.
approaches.time: O(n²) per pass, up to O(n³)

approaches.name: Sort by start + one sweep
approaches.idea: After sorting, compare each interval only with the last merged block.
approaches.space: O(n) — the output plus the sort’s buffer

solution.summary: Sort the intervals by start. Then sweep once: if the next interval starts before or at the end of the last merged block, extend that block's end to the max of both ends; otherwise start a new block. Sorting makes it O(n log n).
solution.explanation:
**Why sort by start?** After sorting, any interval that overlaps the current merged block must come **right after** it — an interval that starts later than the block's end cannot be bridged by anything that follows, because everything after it starts even later.

**Algorithm**
1. Sort by `start`.
2. For each `[start, end]`:
   - if `merged` is non-empty and `start ≤ last.end` → overlap: `last.end = max(last.end, end)`;
   - else push `[start, end]` as a new block.
3. Return `merged`.

**Why `max`?** A block can fully contain the next interval: `[1, 10]` then `[2, 3]` must stay `[1, 10]`, not shrink to `[1, 3]`.

**Touching intervals.** Use `≤` if `[1, 4]` and `[4, 5]` should merge (the usual definition); use `<` if they should stay separate. Ask the interviewer.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) for the sort + O(n) sweep. Output can be n intervals.

**Real uses:** merging busy slots in a calendar ("find free time"), combining overlapping IP ranges or log time windows, coalescing booked seat ranges.

complexity.time: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the sweep is O(n)
complexity.space: O(n) for the output (plus the sort's internal space)

keyPoints: Sort by start so overlaps are adjacent
Compare only with the last merged block
Extend with max(last.end, end) — containment case
Clarify whether touching intervals merge (≤ vs <)
O(n log n) because of the sort

visuals.title: Sort + sweep on [[8,10],[1,3],[15,18],[2,6],[9,12]]
visuals.caption: One lane per input interval (sorted by start); the bottom lane holds the merged blocks. Blue = current interval, orange = block being extended.

steps.note: Input arrives unsorted: [8,10] [1,3] [15,18] [2,6] [9,12]. **Sort by start** so every interval that can overlap the current block comes right after it (lanes are drawn in sorted order).
[1,3]: `merged` is empty, so it becomes the first block.
[2,6]: start 2 ≤ last block's end 3 → **overlap**. Extend the block to end = max(3, 6) = 6.
[8,10]: start 8 > last block's end 6 → there is a **gap**, and because the list is sorted nothing later can bridge it. Start a new block.
[9,12]: start 9 ≤ last block's end 10 → **overlap**. Extend the block to end = max(10, 12) = 12.
[15,18]: start 15 > last block's end 12 → there is a **gap**, and because the list is sorted nothing later can bridge it. Start a new block.
Result: [1,6], [8,12], [15,18]. Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time; the pass is O(n).

rows: Extend the last block or start a new one
Before / overlap / after in one pass
Keep if start ≥ last kept end
Earliest end leaves the most room

pitfalls: Forgetting to sort, or sorting by end
Setting last.end = end instead of max(last.end, end) — breaks containment like [1,10],[2,3]
Using < when touching intervals should merge
Mutating the input array in place when the caller needs it — copy first if required

followUps.question: Intervals arrive one by one in a stream. How do you keep them merged?
followUps.answer: Keep them in a balanced BST / TreeMap keyed by start; on insert, find the neighbours that overlap, merge them, and remove the absorbed ones — O(log n) amortised per insert.

followUps.question: Find the free time common to several people's calendars.
followUps.answer: Put all busy intervals together, merge them, and report the gaps between consecutive merged blocks.

questions.title: Insert Interval
questions.prompt: `intervals` is a list of **non-overlapping** intervals sorted by start. Insert `newInterval` so that the list stays sorted and non-overlapping, merging wherever needed, and return the new list.
constraints: intervals is sorted by start and non-overlapping
hints: You could append the new interval and run Merge Intervals. What does that cost, and what does it ignore?
Relative to the new interval, every existing interval is entirely before it, overlapping it, or entirely after it — and they appear in that order.
Copy intervals with end < new.start; absorb those with start ≤ new.end (min of starts, max of ends); push the merged one; copy the rest.

approaches.name: Append + Merge Intervals
approaches.idea: Add newInterval, sort, merge. Correct but ignores that the input is already sorted.

approaches.name: Binary search + merge
approaches.idea: Find the insertion range with binary search; still O(n) to build the output array.

approaches.name: Three-phase linear scan
approaches.idea: Before / overlapping / after in one pass.

solution.summary: Because the list is sorted and non-overlapping, one pass has three phases: copy intervals that end before the new one starts, absorb every interval that starts before the new one ends by taking the min start and max end, push the merged interval, then copy the rest. O(n) time.
solution.explanation:
**Three phases** (they always occur in this order because the input is sorted):
1. **Before:** `intervals[i].end < start` → entirely to the left, copy it.
2. **Overlap:** `intervals[i].start ≤ end` → it touches or overlaps the new interval: `start = min(start, it.start)`, `end = max(end, it.end)`. Keep absorbing — the new interval may swallow several.
3. Push the merged `[start, end]`, then **after:** copy every remaining interval.

**Why the conditions are exactly these.** Phase 1 uses `end < start` (strict) so a touching interval like `[1, 4]` with new `[4, 6]` falls into phase 2 and merges. Phase 2 uses `start ≤ end` for the same reason.

**Edge cases:** empty list → `[newInterval]`; new interval before everything (phase 1 empty) or after everything (phase 2 and 3 empty); new interval swallowing all intervals.

**Complexity.** Every interval is visited once: O(n). Binary search could find the overlap range in O(log n), but building the output is still O(n) in an array-based language.

code.code:
def insert(intervals, new_interval):
    result = []
    start, end = new_interval
    i, n = 0, len(intervals)
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < start:  # ends before the new one starts
        result.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= end:  # overlaps: absorb it
        start = min(start, intervals[i][0])
        end = max(end, intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    result.append([start, end])  # the merged new interval
    result.extend(intervals[i:])  # start after the new one ends
    return result

complexity.time: O(n) — each interval is examined once

keyPoints: Use the given order — no sort needed, O(n)
Three phases: before (end < start), overlap (start ≤ end), after
Merging = min of starts, max of ends
Touching intervals merge — mind < vs ≤
Handle empty input and insert-at-ends cases

visuals.title: Inserting [4,8] into [[1,2],[3,5],[6,7],[8,10],[12,16]]
visuals.caption: Blue = copied as is, red = absorbed into the new interval, orange = the new interval growing, green = the result.

steps.note: The existing intervals are sorted and do not overlap. The new interval [4,8] must be placed and merged with everything it touches. One left-to-right pass, three phases.
**Phase 1 (before):** [1,2] ends at 2 < 4, so it lies completely to the left of the new interval → copy it to the result.
**Phase 2 (overlap):** [3,5] starts at 3 ≤ end 8 → absorb it: start = min(4, 3) = 3, end = max(8, 5) = 8.
**Phase 2 (overlap):** [6,7] starts at 6 ≤ end 8 → absorb it: start = min(3, 6) = 3, end = max(8, 7) = 8.
**Phase 2 (overlap):** [8,10] starts at 8 ≤ end 8 (touching counts as overlap) → absorb it: start = min(3, 8) = 3, end = max(8, 10) = 10.
[12,16] starts at 12 > 10, so phase 2 stops. Push the merged interval [3,10] — the red intervals were absorbed into it.
**Phase 3 (after):** [12,16] starts after 10 → copy it unchanged.
Result [1,2], [3,10], [12,16]. Each interval was looked at once → O(n); no sorting needed because the input was already sorted.

visuals.title: Insert Interval vs re-running Merge Intervals
rows: Uses the fact that input is sorted?
Handled by end < start (phase 1) and start ≤ end (phase 2)

pitfalls: Using ≤ in phase 1, so a touching interval is copied instead of merged
Stopping after absorbing a single interval — the new one may swallow several
Forgetting to push the merged interval when phase 2 absorbed nothing
Sorting again — wastes the O(n) opportunity

followUps.question: What if you must insert many intervals one at a time?
followUps.answer: Keep the intervals in a TreeMap / balanced BST keyed by start so each insert finds and merges neighbours in O(log n + merged count).

followUps.question: Remove an interval instead (cut [a, b] out of the list)?
followUps.answer: Same scan: intervals fully outside are copied; overlapping ones are trimmed to their parts left of a and right of b (an interval can split into two).

questions.title: Non-overlapping Intervals (minimum removals)
questions.prompt:
Given a list of intervals `[start, end]`, return the **minimum number of intervals to remove** so that the remaining intervals do not overlap.

Intervals that only touch (`[1, 2]` and `[2, 3]`) do **not** overlap.
hints: Minimising removals is the same as maximising the number of intervals you keep.
If you had to pick the first meeting to keep, which one leaves the most room for everything else?
Sort by end; keep an interval if its start ≥ the end of the last kept one, otherwise count it as removed.

approaches.name: Try all subsets
approaches.idea: Check every subset for overlaps and keep the largest valid one.

approaches.name: DP like LIS
approaches.idea: Sort by start; dp[i] = max kept ending with i = 1 + max dp[j] for compatible j.

approaches.name: Greedy by earliest end
approaches.idea: Sort by end; keep every interval that starts at or after the last kept end.

solution.summary: Minimising removals = maximising kept intervals, which is activity selection. Sort by end time and greedily keep each interval that starts at or after the last kept end; everything else is removed. The earliest-ending interval is always safe to keep, so this is optimal in O(n log n).
solution.explanation:
**Reframe:** removed = n − (maximum number of non-overlapping intervals you can keep).

**Greedy choice:** among all intervals, keep the one that **ends first**. Then discard everything that overlaps it and repeat on the rest.

**Why it is safe (exchange argument).** Take any optimal set of kept intervals and look at its first interval `X`. The greedy pick `G` ends no later than `X` (it ends first overall). Replace `X` by `G`: `G` ends earlier, so it cannot collide with anything that came after `X`. The set is still valid and has the same size — so some optimal answer starts with `G`. Repeat the argument for the rest.

**Algorithm**
1. Sort by end.
2. `lastEnd = −∞`. For each `[start, end]`: if `start ≥ lastEnd` keep it (`lastEnd = end`), else `removed++`.

**Why not sort by start?** `[[1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5]]`: by start you keep `[1, 10]` first and must remove the other two (2 removals); by end you keep `[2, 3]` and `[4, 5]` and remove only `[1, 10]`. (Sorting by start works only if, on overlap, you keep the one with the smaller end — which is the same idea.)

**Related:** "Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons" is the same greedy (count kept groups instead of removals).

complexity.time: O(n log n) — sorting; the sweep is O(n)

keyPoints: Min removals = n − max non-overlapping intervals (activity selection)
Sort by END, not by start
Keep if start ≥ lastEnd (touching is allowed)
Exchange argument proves the earliest finisher is safe
O(n log n)

visuals.title: Keep the earliest finisher on [[3,6],[1,4],[6,8],[2,3],[5,7]]
visuals.caption: Lanes are sorted by end time. Green = kept, red = removed, grey = not processed yet.

steps.note: Input [3,6] [1,4] [6,8] [2,3] [5,7]. **Sort by end time**: the interval that finishes first leaves the most room for the rest, so it is always safe to keep.
[2,3]: start 2 ≥ lastEnd −∞ → **keep** it; lastEnd = 3.
[1,4]: start 1 < lastEnd 3 → it overlaps the kept interval, which ends **earlier** (3 ≤ 4). Dropping this one is never worse. removed = 1.
[3,6]: start 3 ≥ lastEnd 3 (touching is fine) → **keep** it; lastEnd = 6.
[5,7]: start 5 < lastEnd 6 → it overlaps the kept interval, which ends **earlier** (6 ≤ 7). Dropping this one is never worse. removed = 2.
[6,8]: start 6 ≥ lastEnd 6 (touching is fine) → **keep** it; lastEnd = 8.
Kept 3 intervals ([2,3], [3,6], [6,8]), removed **2**. This is the classic activity-selection greedy: max kept = n − min removed. O(n log n) for the sort.

visuals.title: Sort key matters: [[1,10],[2,3],[4,5]]
rows: Sort by start, keep the first seen
Sort by length, keep the shortest first
Here yes — but fails on [[1,5],[4,7],[6,10]]: keeps [4,7] alone (2 removals) instead of [1,5],[6,10] (1)
Sort by end, keep the earliest finisher

pitfalls: Sorting by start and always keeping the first interval
Treating touching intervals ([1,2], [2,3]) as overlapping
Initialising lastEnd to 0 when starts can be negative
Returning the number kept instead of the number removed

followUps.question: Return the maximum number of meetings one person can attend.
followUps.answer: That is the kept count from the same greedy: n − removed.

followUps.question: Minimum arrows to burst balloons (each arrow at x bursts every [s, e] with s ≤ x ≤ e).
followUps.answer: Sort by end; shoot at the first end; skip balloons with start ≤ that end; shoot again at the next balloon's end. Count the shots. (Here touching balloons share an arrow.)

questions.title: Meeting Rooms II (minimum rooms)
questions.pattern: Sort by start + min-heap of end times
questions.prompt:
Given meeting time intervals `[start, end]`, return the **minimum number of conference rooms** needed so that every meeting can take place.

A meeting that ends at time `t` frees its room for a meeting that starts at `t`.

examples.explanation: [0,30] needs its own room; [5,10] and [15,20] can share one
At time 5, [2,6], [4,7] and [5,9] are all running

hints: The answer is the maximum number of meetings happening at the same moment.
Process meetings by start time. When a new meeting starts, which existing room is the best candidate to reuse?
Keep a min-heap of end times: if the smallest end ≤ start, pop it (reuse that room); always push the new end. The answer is the heap size.

approaches.name: Count at every time point
approaches.idea: For each meeting start, count how many meetings contain that moment.

approaches.name: Sort + min-heap of end times
approaches.idea: Reuse the room that frees up earliest; open a new room when none is free.

approaches.name: Chronological sweep
approaches.idea: Sort starts and ends separately; two pointers: a start before the next end → +1 room, otherwise −1. Track the max.

solution.summary: Sort meetings by start time and keep a min-heap of end times for rooms in use. For each meeting, if the earliest-ending room is free by its start, pop it and reuse the room; then push this meeting's end. The heap size at the end is the peak number of overlapping meetings — the answer — in O(n log n).
solution.explanation:
**Key insight:** the minimum number of rooms equals the **maximum number of meetings running at the same time**.

**Greedy with a heap**
1. Sort meetings by start.
2. A min-heap `ends` stores the end time of each room's current meeting.
3. For each meeting `[start, end]`:
   - if the smallest end ≤ `start`, that room is free → pop it (reuse the room);
   - push `end` (the meeting now occupies a room).
4. Return `ends.size()`.

**Why reuse the room that frees up earliest?** If any room is free at `start`, the earliest-ending one is. Using it never hurts later meetings: all other rooms stay busy exactly as long as before.

**Why is the final heap size the answer?** Each meeting pops at most one and pushes exactly one, so the size never decreases; it grows by one exactly when all rooms are busy at a meeting's start — i.e. when the overlap count hits a new maximum.

**Alternative: chronological sweep.** Sort all starts and all ends separately. Walk the starts; if `start < ends[j]` a new room is needed (`rooms++`), else a meeting finished (`j++`, reuse). Same O(n log n), no heap — good to mention as a follow-up.

**Real uses:** booking meeting rooms, counting concurrent calls/connections, assigning CPU cores or delivery riders to jobs.

complexity.time: O(n log n) — sorting plus one heap push/pop per meeting
complexity.space: O(n) — the heap can hold every meeting

keyPoints: Answer = maximum number of simultaneous meetings
Sort by start; min-heap of end times for occupied rooms
Reuse the room that frees up earliest (heap minimum) if it ends ≤ start
Heap size never shrinks → final size = answer
Mention the two-sorted-arrays sweep as an alternative

visuals.title: Assigning rooms with a min-heap of end times
visuals.caption: Each lane is a room. A room is reused when its last meeting ends at or before the next start (the heap minimum).

steps.note: Meetings [7,8] [1,4] [5,9] [2,6] [8,10] [4,7] are **sorted by start** and handled in that order. The min-heap `ends` holds the end time of every meeting that is still occupying a room.
[1,4]: no room in use yet → open Room 1. Push its end 4.
[2,6]: the earliest end is 4 > 2 — **every room is still busy**, so open Room 2. Push 6.
[4,7]: the earliest end in the heap is 4 ≤ 4, so that meeting is over — **pop** it and reuse Room 1. Push 7.
[5,9]: the earliest end is 6 > 5 — **every room is still busy**, so open Room 3. Push 9.
[7,8]: the earliest end in the heap is 6 ≤ 7, so that meeting is over — **pop** it and reuse Room 2. Push 8.
[8,10]: the earliest end in the heap is 7 ≤ 8, so that meeting is over — **pop** it and reuse Room 1. Push 10.

Done: the heap holds 3 end times → **3 rooms**. The heap never shrinks (each pop is followed by a push), so its final size is the peak number of simultaneous meetings — here [2,6], [4,7] and [5,9] all run at time 5.

visuals.title: Three ways to count rooms
rows: For each start, count meetings covering it
Reuse the earliest-free room, else open one
Two pointers: next event is a start (+1) or an end (−1)
Tells you which room each meeting uses?
A meeting covers time t when start ≤ t < end
start < end → new room, else reuse

pitfalls: Using < instead of ≤ when checking whether the earliest meeting has ended (touching meetings can share a room)
Popping all finished meetings and then returning the final heap size — then the size is no longer the peak; track a max instead
Sorting by end instead of start
JavaScript has no built-in heap — be ready to write a small one or use the two-array sweep

followUps.question: Meeting Rooms I: can one person attend all meetings?
followUps.answer: Sort by start and check that every start ≥ the previous end. O(n log n).

followUps.question: Solve it without a heap.
followUps.answer: Sort starts and ends separately; walk starts with pointer i and ends with pointer j: if starts[i] < ends[j] rooms++ else j++. Answer = rooms (or the max of a running counter).

followUps.question: Return which room each meeting gets.
followUps.answer: Store [end, roomId] in the heap; when reusing, give the meeting the popped roomId, otherwise a new id.

questions.title: Jump Game
questions.prompt:
You start at index 0 of an array `nums` of non-negative integers. `nums[i]` is the **maximum** jump length from index `i` (you may jump any distance from 1 up to `nums[i]`).

Return `true` if you can reach the **last index**, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: Every path lands on index 3, where the jump length is 0

hints: You do not need the actual path — only whether the last index is reachable.
If you can reach index i, you can also reach every index before it. So the reachable set is always a prefix 0..reach.
Scan left to right keeping reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]); if you ever see i > reach, you are stuck.

approaches.name: Backtracking
approaches.idea: From each index try every jump length recursively.

approaches.name: DP (good indices)
approaches.idea: From right to left, good[i] = some j in (i, i + nums[i]] is good.

approaches.name: Greedy farthest reach
approaches.idea: Track the farthest reachable index in one pass.

solution.summary: The reachable indices always form a prefix, so I only track reach — the farthest index reachable so far. Scanning left to right, if i > reach I am stuck and return false; otherwise reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]), and once reach covers the last index I return true. One pass, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Key observation.** If index `k` is reachable, every index `j < k` is reachable too (you could have jumped shorter). So "what is reachable" is fully described by one number: `reach`, the farthest reachable index.

**Algorithm**
1. `reach = 0`.
2. For `i = 0, 1, …`:
   - if `i > reach` → `i` cannot be reached, and nothing beyond it either → `false`;
   - `reach = max(reach, i + nums[i])`;
   - if `reach ≥ n − 1` → `true`.

**Why is greedy enough?** We never commit to a specific jump; `reach` summarises *all* possible paths at once. Each index updates it in O(1).

**Example `[3, 2, 1, 0, 4]`:** reach becomes 3, 3, 3, 3 — every index can only reach index 3, whose value is 0. At `i = 4`, `4 > 3` → false.

**Alternative view (backwards greedy):** keep `goal = n − 1`; scanning from the right, if `i + nums[i] ≥ goal` then `goal = i`. Answer: `goal === 0`.
keyPoints: Reachable indices form a prefix → track only reach
If i > reach you are stuck: return false
reach = max(reach, i + nums[i])
Early exit when reach ≥ last index
Mention the O(n²) DP and why greedy beats it

visuals.title: Reachable on nums = [1, 3, 0, 0, 2, 0, 1]
visuals.caption: The band is every index reachable so far. Zeros inside the band are harmless — we simply jump over them.

steps.note: Start at index 0 with `reach = 0`. `reach` is the farthest index we can get to using any jumps from the indices seen so far; everything up to it is reachable.
`i = 0` (≤ reach, so we can stand here). From here the farthest index we can reach is 1, so `reach = max(0, 0 + 1) = 1`.
`i = 1` (≤ reach, so we can stand here). From here the farthest index we can reach is 4, so `reach = max(1, 1 + 3) = 4`.
`i = 2` (≤ reach, so we can stand here). From here the farthest index we can reach is 2, so `reach = max(4, 2 + 0) = 4`. No improvement — that is fine as long as i stays ≤ reach.
`i = 3` (≤ reach, so we can stand here). From here the farthest index we can reach is 3, so `reach = max(4, 3 + 0) = 4`. No improvement — that is fine as long as i stays ≤ reach.
`i = 4` (≤ reach, so we can stand here). From here the farthest index we can reach is 6, so `reach = max(4, 4 + 2) = 6`. reach ≥ 6 → **return true**.
Answer **true**. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space — no need to try every jump length.

visuals.title: Stuck on nums = [3, 2, 1, 0, 4]
visuals.caption: Every path lands on index 3 (value 0). The reach never passes 3, so index 4 is unreachable.

steps.note: Start at index 0 with `reach = 0`. `reach` is the farthest index we can get to using any jumps from the indices seen so far; everything up to it is reachable.
`i = 0` (≤ reach, so we can stand here). From here the farthest index we can reach is 3, so `reach = max(0, 0 + 3) = 3`.
`i = 1` (≤ reach, so we can stand here). From here the farthest index we can reach is 3, so `reach = max(3, 1 + 2) = 3`. No improvement — that is fine as long as i stays ≤ reach.
`i = 2` (≤ reach, so we can stand here). From here the farthest index we can reach is 3, so `reach = max(3, 2 + 1) = 3`. No improvement — that is fine as long as i stays ≤ reach.
`i = 3` (≤ reach, so we can stand here). From here the farthest index we can reach is 3, so `reach = max(3, 3 + 0) = 3`. No improvement — that is fine as long as i stays ≤ reach.
`i = 4` but `reach = 3`: no jump from indices 0..3 gets past 3 (nums[3] = 0 is a trap). Index 4 is unreachable → **return false**.

pitfalls: Always taking the longest jump from the current index (that is a different, wrong greedy — [2, 3, 1, 1, 4] still works but [3, 1, 4, 0, 0, 0] fails: max jump 3 lands on a 0)
Forgetting the i > reach check, so you "jump" from unreachable indices
Returning false for a single-element array

followUps.question: Jump Game II: minimum number of jumps (always reachable).
followUps.answer: BFS by levels in O(n): track the current level's end and the farthest reach; when i hits the level end, jumps++ and the level end = farthest.

followUps.question: From index i you may jump exactly nums[i] forwards or backwards; can you reach any index holding 0 (Jump Game III)?
followUps.answer: Greedy reach no longer applies. Treat indices as graph nodes with up to two edges each and run BFS/DFS from the start with a visited set: O(n).

questions.title: Gas Station
questions.pattern: Greedy reset on negative running sum
questions.prompt:
There are `n` gas stations on a **circular** road. Station `i` gives you `gas[i]` fuel, and driving from station `i` to station `i + 1` (the last one wraps to 0) costs `cost[i]` fuel. Your tank starts empty and has no capacity limit.

Return the index of the station where you can start and drive **once around the whole circle**, or `-1` if no such station exists. If a solution exists, it is guaranteed to be unique.

examples.explanation: From 0 the tank goes 1, 0, then −2 at station 2, so stations 0–2 are all ruled out

hints: Simulating from every start is O(n²). When is the answer obviously -1?
If total gas ≥ total cost, a valid start exists. If you start at s and run out before reaching i + 1, what does that say about starts between s and i?
Keep a running tank; when it goes negative at i, the next candidate is i + 1 and the tank resets. Return the last candidate if the overall total ≥ 0.

approaches.name: Simulate every start
approaches.idea: For each station, drive around and check the tank never drops below 0.

approaches.name: One-pass greedy
approaches.idea: Reset the candidate to i + 1 whenever the tank goes negative; total ≥ 0 decides existence.

solution.summary: If total gas is less than total cost, return -1. Otherwise scan once with a running tank from a candidate start; whenever the tank goes negative at station i, no start between the candidate and i can work, so move the candidate to i + 1 and reset the tank. The final candidate is the answer — O(n) time, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Simplify:** only `diff[i] = gas[i] − cost[i]` matters.

**Fact 1 — existence.** If `sum(diff) < 0`, no start works: you need more fuel than exists. If `sum(diff) ≥ 0`, some start works (start right after the lowest point of the running total — see the second visual).

**Fact 2 — skipping.** Suppose you start at `s` and the tank first goes negative after station `i`. Any start `k` with `s < k ≤ i` would arrive at `i` with **no more** fuel than starting at `s`: the stretch `s..k−1` had a non-negative sum (the tank had not gone negative before `i`), so dropping it can only remove fuel. Therefore none of `s..i` works, and the next candidate is `i + 1`.

**Algorithm**
1. `total = tank = 0`, `start = 0`.
2. For each `i`: add `diff[i]` to both; if `tank < 0` → `start = i + 1`, `tank = 0`.
3. Return `total ≥ 0 ? start : −1`.

**Why don't we need to wrap around to check the final start?** Fact 1 guarantees a solution exists when `total ≥ 0`, and Fact 2 eliminated every other station, so the remaining candidate must be it.

code.code:
def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
    total = 0  # net gas over the whole loop
    tank = 0   # net gas since the current candidate start
    start = 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        diff = gas[i] - cost[i]
        total += diff
        tank += diff
        if tank < 0:  # cannot reach station i + 1 from start
            start = i + 1  # no station in [start, i] can be the answer
            tank = 0
    return start if total >= 0 else -1

keyPoints: Total gas < total cost → -1; otherwise a start exists
When the tank goes negative at i, skip every start up to i
Candidate = i + 1 and reset the tank
No second loop needed — explain why
Equivalent: start right after the minimum prefix sum

visuals.title: One pass on gas = [3, 1, 1, 5, 2], cost = [2, 2, 3, 1, 2]
visuals.caption: Light blue = the stretch driven since the current candidate start. Red = the station where the tank went negative.

steps.note: At station i you gain `gas[i]` and spend `cost[i]` to drive to i + 1, so only `diff = gas[i] − cost[i]` matters. `start` is the current candidate; `tank` is the fuel collected since `start`.
`i = 0`: diff = 1, tank = 1 ≥ 0 — still fine from start 0.
`i = 1`: diff = -1, tank = 0 ≥ 0 — still fine from start 0.

`i = 2`: diff = -2, tank = -2 < 0 — starting at 0 we cannot reach station 3. Every start in [0, 2] would arrive here with no more fuel (and also fail), so jump the candidate to **start = 3** and reset tank to 0.
`i = 3`: diff = 4, tank = 4 ≥ 0 — still fine from start 3.
`i = 4`: diff = 0, tank = 4 ≥ 0 — still fine from start 3.
total = 2 ≥ 0, so a full loop is possible and the answer is the last candidate: **start = 3**. (If total were negative, no start could work → -1.) One pass: O(n) time, O(1) space.

visuals.title: Proof picture: start right after the lowest running total
visuals.caption: In the last step the bottom row shows, under each station, the tank after driving that station’s leg when the trip starts at station 3.

steps.note: Why does the one-pass trick work? Look at the **running total** of `diff` if we start at station 0.
Running total from station 0: 1, 0, -2, 2, 2. It dips below zero, so station 0 fails.
The lowest point is -2 after station 2. Starting right **after** the lowest point means every later running total is measured from the bottom, so it can never go negative.

Start at station 3 and drive the full loop (3 → 4 → 0 → 1 → 2): the tank is 4, 4, 5, 4, 2 — never negative, ending at total = 2 ≥ 0. The bottom row shows the same values under each station’s index. This is exactly the start the greedy found by resetting whenever tank < 0.

pitfalls: Simulating from every station (O(n²)) without the skipping argument
Forgetting the total check and returning a start that cannot complete the loop
Resetting start to i instead of i + 1
Thinking you must verify the final start with a second loop

followUps.question: Is the "lowest running sum" view the same algorithm?
followUps.answer: Yes. Write the running sums of diff starting with the 0 before station 0 (0, diff[0], diff[0] + diff[1], …). When the total is ≥ 0, starting at the station right after the first lowest running sum works, because every later running total is measured from that bottom. The reset-when-negative loop moves start exactly when the running sum reaches a new lowest value, so it ends on that same station.

followUps.question: Return all valid starts when uniqueness is not guaranteed.
followUps.answer: Every start s where the running total from s never goes negative: compute prefix sums over the doubled array and use a sliding-window minimum, O(n).

questions.title: Partition Labels
questions.pattern: Last occurrence + extend the current part
questions.prompt:
Split the string `s` (lowercase letters) into **as many parts as possible** so that each letter appears in **at most one** part. Concatenating the parts in order must give back `s`.

Return the list of part sizes.

examples.explanation: 'e' at both ends forces one part

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: If a part contains the letter x, where must that part end at the earliest?
Record the last index of every letter first.
Scan with end = max(end, last[s[i]]); when i === end, close the part and start a new one at i + 1.

approaches.name: Try every cut
approaches.idea: For each possible cut position check that no letter appears on both sides; repeat greedily.

approaches.name: Intervals per letter + merge
approaches.idea: Build [first, last] per letter and run Merge Intervals; sizes are the merged lengths.

approaches.name: Last index + one pass
approaches.idea: Extend the current part to the last occurrence of each letter seen; cut when i reaches end.

solution.summary: First record the last index of every letter. Then scan, extending the current part's end to the last occurrence of each letter I see; when the index reaches that end, every letter in the part is complete, so I cut and start the next part. Two linear passes, O(1) extra space for 26 letters.
solution.explanation:
**Observation.** If a part contains letter `x`, it must extend at least to the **last** `x` in the string. So while scanning a part, keep `end` = the furthest last-occurrence of any letter seen so far in this part.

**Algorithm**
1. `last[c]` = last index of each letter (one pass).
2. `start = end = 0`. For each `i`:
   - `end = max(end, last[s[i]])`;
   - if `i === end`: all letters in `s[start..end]` finish inside it → record `end − start + 1`, set `start = i + 1`.

**Why greedy (cut as early as possible) maximises the count.** Cutting at the first valid position never blocks a later cut — the remaining suffix is unchanged, and any valid partition must have its first cut at or after this point. So the earliest cut is always part of some optimal answer.

**Connection to intervals.** Each letter defines an interval [first, last]. Parts are exactly the merged overlapping intervals — this is Merge Intervals (see the second visual).

code.code:
def partition_labels(s):
    last = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(s)}  # char -> last index
    sizes = []
    start = end = 0
    for i, c in enumerate(s):
        end = max(end, last[c])  # this part must reach c's last copy
        if i == end:  # every char seen so far ends inside [start, end]
            sizes.append(end - start + 1)
            start = i + 1
    return sizes

complexity.space: O(1) — at most 26 entries in the last-index table (plus the output)

keyPoints: A part must reach the last occurrence of every letter in it
Precompute last index per letter
end = max(end, last[s[i]]); cut when i === end
Earliest cut is safe → maximum number of parts
Same as merging per-letter intervals

visuals.title: Partition Labels on s = "abacbddefe"
visuals.caption: Orange band = the part being built (it must reach `end`). Green bands = finished parts.

steps.note: First pass: record the **last index** of every letter. A part that contains a letter must stretch at least to that letter's last occurrence.
`i = 0` ('a'): its last copy is at 2, so the part must extend: `end = 2`.
`i = 1` ('b'): its last copy is at 4, so the part must extend: `end = 4`.
`i = 2` ('a'): last copy at 2 ≤ end 4, nothing changes.
`i = 3` ('c'): last copy at 3 ≤ end 4, nothing changes.
`i = 4` ('b'): i reached `end = 4` — every letter in [0, 4] has its last copy inside, so **cut here**: part size 5.
`i = 5` ('d'): its last copy is at 6, so the part must extend: `end = 6`.
`i = 6` ('d'): i reached `end = 6` — every letter in [5, 6] has its last copy inside, so **cut here**: part size 2.
`i = 7` ('e'): its last copy is at 9, so the part must extend: `end = 9`.
`i = 8` ('f'): last copy at 8 ≤ end 9, nothing changes.
`i = 9` ('e'): i reached `end = 9` — every letter in [7, 9] has its last copy inside, so **cut here**: part size 3.
Sizes **[5, 2, 3]**: "abacb" | "dd" | "efe". Cutting as early as possible gives the maximum number of parts. O(n) time, O(1) space (26 letters).

visuals.title: Letters as intervals → merge them
visuals.caption: Each lane is a letter's span in "abacbddefe"; the bottom lane shows the merged parts.

steps.note: Another way to see it: draw each letter as a bar from its **first** to its **last** occurrence (bar covers indices first..last). A part may not cut through any bar.
Bars 'a', 'b', 'c' are chained together ('b' overlaps both 'a' and 'c'), so they must share one part: indices 0..4, size 5.
Bar 'd' overlaps no other bar, so it is a part on its own: indices 5..6, size 2.
Bars 'e', 'f' overlap each other, so they must share one part: indices 7..9, size 3.

So Partition Labels is **Merge Intervals** in disguise: one interval per letter, merge the overlapping ones, report the lengths. The one-pass `end` pointer does the same without building the intervals.

pitfalls: Cutting when a letter repeats instead of when i reaches the furthest last index
Returning the substrings when sizes are asked (or vice versa)
Forgetting to update start = i + 1 after a cut

followUps.question: Return the parts themselves?
followUps.answer: Record (start, end) at each cut and slice s — same O(n).

followUps.question: What if the alphabet is Unicode?
followUps.answer: Use a hash map for last instead of an int[26]; complexity stays O(n) time, O(k) space for k distinct characters.

questions.title: Greedy vs Dynamic Programming — how do you choose?
questions.prompt: "What is the difference between a **greedy** algorithm and **dynamic programming**? How do you know when greedy is correct? Give an example where greedy fails."
hints: Both rely on optimal substructure. What extra property does greedy need?
Greedy commits to one choice per step; DP compares all choices using stored sub-answers.
Coin change with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6 is a short counter-example. For a proof of greedy, use an exchange argument.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Greedy picks the best option each step and DP stores results." No property names, no proof idea, no counter-example.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Names the greedy-choice property, explains the exchange argument, gives a counter-example (coins [1, 3, 4] for 6), contrasts complexity, and lists classic problems for each technique.

solution.summary: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never revisits it; it is correct only when the problem has the greedy-choice property — some optimal solution always starts with that local choice. Dynamic programming instead tries every choice and reuses stored answers to overlapping subproblems, so it is correct whenever optimal substructure holds, at a higher cost. Coin change with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6 shows greedy failing (3 coins vs 2).
solution.explanation:
### Greedy
- Builds the answer step by step, each time taking the choice that looks best **right now** (earliest end, largest coin, farthest reach).
- **Never undoes** a choice → usually just *sort + one pass*: O(n log n) or O(n).
- Correct only if the problem has:
  1. **Greedy-choice property** — there is an optimal solution that begins with the greedy choice;
  2. **Optimal substructure** — after making that choice, the rest is the same problem on a smaller input.

### Dynamic programming
- Needs **optimal substructure** + **overlapping subproblems**.
- At each state it **tries every choice** and takes the best, using stored answers (memo/table).
- Always correct when the recurrence is right, but costs *states × choices* (e.g. O(amount · k) for coins, O(n · W) for knapsack).

### How to prove greedy is correct
- **Exchange argument:** take any optimal solution; swap its first choice for the greedy choice and show it is still valid and no worse. Example: interval scheduling — the interval that ends first can replace the first interval of any optimal schedule.
- **Greedy stays ahead:** show that after every step, greedy's partial solution is at least as good as any other (Jump Game's `reach`).

### How to show greedy is wrong
Find a **small counter-example**. Coins [1, 3, 4], amount 6: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins), optimal is 3 + 3 (2 coins). 0/1 knapsack: best value/weight ratio first can leave the bag half empty.

### Classic split
| Greedy works | Needs DP |
|---|---|
| Activity selection / non-overlapping intervals (earliest end) | 0/1 knapsack |
| Fractional knapsack (best ratio) | Coin change with arbitrary coins |
| Jump Game (farthest reach), Gas Station | Longest increasing subsequence |
| Huffman coding, Dijkstra (non-negative edges), Kruskal/Prim MST | Edit distance, LCS |
| Coin change with canonical coins (1, 5, 10, 25) | House Robber |

### Interview strategy
1. Propose the greedy idea if one is natural, then **immediately test it on 2–3 tiny tricky inputs**.
2. If you find a counter-example, say so and switch to DP (state, transition, base cases).
3. If you keep greedy, give the one-sentence exchange argument — interviewers love hearing *why* it is safe.
keyPoints: Greedy = commit to the locally best choice; DP = compare all choices with stored sub-answers
Greedy needs the greedy-choice property (+ optimal substructure); DP needs overlapping subproblems (+ optimal substructure)
Prove greedy with an exchange argument or "greedy stays ahead"
Disprove greedy with a small counter-example: coins [1, 3, 4], amount 6
Greedy is usually O(n log n); DP costs states × choices

visuals.title: Coins [1, 3, 4], amount 6: greedy commits, DP compares
visuals.caption: Orange = greedy's path / DP's candidates, green = the optimal path, red = greedy's suboptimal path.

steps.note: Make 6 with coins [1, 3, 4]. Every first coin leaves a smaller amount to solve — a tree of choices.
**Greedy** takes the biggest coin that fits, 4, and commits to it forever. 2 is left.
Only coin 1 fits now, twice: 4 + 1 + 1 = **3 coins**. Greedy is fast, but it never questioned its first choice.
**DP** looks at every first coin and uses the stored best answer for what remains: dp[2] = 2, dp[3] = 1, dp[5] = 2. Total = 1 + that.
Best first move is coin 3 (1 + dp[3] = 2), then 3 again: **3 + 3 = 2 coins**. DP was right because it compared all options; greedy's first choice was not part of any optimal answer.

With coins [1, 5, 10, 25] greedy is optimal (a "canonical" system) — that is why cashiers can do it. Whether greedy is safe depends on the input structure, so you must prove it or find a counter-example.

visuals.title: Greedy vs dynamic programming
rows: Take the locally best choice, never reconsider
Try every choice, keep the best using stored results
Sort, then one pass (often with a heap)
Table or memoized recursion over states
O(n log n) or O(n), O(1) extra space
Must be proved (exchange argument); often wrong
Correct whenever the recurrence is correct
Interval scheduling, Huffman, Dijkstra, MST, Jump Game
Knapsack, LIS, LCS, edit distance, coin change

visuals.title: Choosing a technique in the interview

frames.note: A practical decision path. The key step is actively looking for a counter-example before trusting greedy.
The exchange argument for interval scheduling, in four moves. This is the proof style interviewers expect for greedy.
frames.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    a["Take any optimal schedule OPT"] --> b["Let X be its first interval"]
    b --> c["Greedy pick G ends no later than X"]
    c --> d["Swap X for G: still no overlaps, same size"]
    d --> e["So an optimal answer starts with G; repeat on the rest"]

pitfalls: Assuming greedy works because it passes the examples in the prompt
Saying "DP is always better" — greedy is simpler and faster when it is provably correct
Confusing fractional knapsack (greedy) with 0/1 knapsack (DP)
Calling any algorithm that sorts first "greedy" without stating the greedy choice

followUps.question: Is Dijkstra greedy or DP?
followUps.answer: Greedy: it permanently settles the closest unsettled node. It relies on non-negative edges (exchange argument fails with negative weights — then use Bellman-Ford, which is DP over the number of edges).

followUps.question: When does greedy coin change work?
followUps.answer: For canonical coin systems such as 1, 5, 10, 25 or 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 (most real currencies). It has to be checked per system; DP works for any system.

followUps.question: Can a problem be solved by both?
followUps.answer: Yes. Jump Game has an O(n²) DP and an O(n) greedy; activity selection has an O(n²) DP and an O(n log n) greedy. Greedy is the optimisation once you can prove it.

questions.title: Meeting Rooms (Can a Person Attend All?)
questions.prompt:
Given an array of meeting time intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, determine if a single person could attend **all** meetings without any overlap.

Two meetings that touch at an endpoint (such as `[0, 8]` and `[8, 10]`) are **not** considered overlapping.

examples.explanation: The meeting [0, 30] overlaps with both [5, 10] and [15, 20].
After sorting to [[2, 4], [7, 10]], the first ends at 4 before the second starts at 7.

hints: Checking every pair takes O(n²). How can ordering the meetings make overlap detection adjacent?
Sort the intervals by start time ascending.
Once sorted, just check if any meeting starts strictly before the previous meeting ends (`intervals[i][0] < intervals[i - 1][1]`).

approaches.name: Brute-force all pairs
approaches.idea: Compare every pair of intervals `(i, j)` and check if `max(start_i, start_j) < min(end_i, end_j)`.

approaches.name: Sort by start time + linear scan (Optimal)
approaches.idea: Sort intervals by `start` time. Walk from index `1` to `n - 1`; if `intervals[i][0] < intervals[i - 1][1]`, two consecutive meetings overlap, so return `false`.

solution.summary: Sort meetings by start time in O(n log n), then scan adjacent pairs: if any meeting starts before the previous one ends (`curr.start < prev.end`), return `false`; otherwise return `true`.
solution.explanation:
If a schedule has any conflict at all, then after sorting meetings by start time, there **must** be a conflict between two consecutive meetings in the sorted order.

1. Sort `intervals` ascending by `start` (`a[0] - b[0]`).
2. Loop `i` from `1` to `intervals.length - 1`:
   - Compare `intervals[i][0]` (current start) with `intervals[i - 1][1]` (previous end).
   - If `intervals[i][0] < intervals[i - 1][1]`, they overlap — return `false` immediately.
3. If the loop finishes without conflicts, return `true`.

complexity.time: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting the intervals.
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary (or O(log n) stack space used by the built-in sort).

keyPoints: Clarify boundary touching: `[0, 8]` and `[8, 10]` do NOT overlap, so use strict `<` (`intervals[i][0] < intervals[i - 1][1]`).
Empty or single-element arrays naturally return `true` because the loop body never executes.
This is the warm-up to **Meeting Rooms II**, where instead of returning a boolean you count the minimum number of rooms needed.

visuals.title: Overlap check on [[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]]
visuals.caption: Sort by start time and compare each meeting’s start with the previous meeting’s end.

steps.note: Sort meetings by start time: `[0, 30]`, `[5, 10]`, `[15, 20]`. Start scanning at `i = 1`.
Compare M1 `[5, 10]` with M0 `[0, 30]`: since `currStart (5) < prevEnd (30)`, the two meetings overlap! Return `false`.

pitfalls: Using `<=` instead of `<` when checking overlap — back-to-back meetings like `[2, 4]` and `[4, 7]` are valid.
Using `a[0] > b[0]` in JavaScript `.sort()` instead of `a[0] - b[0]`.

followUps.question: What if you need to find the minimum number of conference rooms required to hold all meetings?
followUps.answer: That is **Meeting Rooms II**: use a min-heap of end times or a two-pointer sweep over sorted start and end arrays in O(n log n) time.

quiz.question: Which property must a problem have for a greedy algorithm to be correct?
options: Greedy-choice property: some optimal solution starts with the locally best choice
The input must already be sorted
quiz.explanation: Greedy commits to its first choice, so that choice must be part of some optimal solution (plus optimal substructure for the rest). Overlapping subproblems is what makes DP useful, not greedy.

quiz.question: Merge Intervals: before the single sweep, what do you sort by?
quiz.explanation: Sorting by start puts every interval that can overlap the current block right after it, so comparing with the last merged block is enough.

quiz.question: Non-overlapping Intervals (minimum removals): which greedy is correct?
options: Sort by start; keep the first interval seen
Sort by end; keep each interval that starts at or after the last kept end
Sort by length; keep the shortest first
Sort by start; keep the longest interval
quiz.explanation: Keeping the earliest finisher leaves the most room for the rest (exchange argument). Sorting by start fails on [[1,10],[2,3],[4,5]]: it keeps [1,10] and removes two instead of one.

quiz.question: Meeting Rooms II: how many rooms do [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]] need?
quiz.explanation: [0,30] overlaps both others, but [5,10] and [15,20] do not overlap each other, so they share a second room. At most two meetings run at once.

quiz.question: In the min-heap solution to Meeting Rooms II, what does the heap size equal after all meetings are processed?
options: The number of meetings that overlap nothing
The maximum number of meetings running at the same time
quiz.explanation: Each meeting pops at most one end and always pushes one, so the size never shrinks; it grows only when every room is busy at a start — i.e. when concurrency reaches a new maximum.

quiz.question: Jump Game on nums = [3, 2, 1, 0, 4]: what is the final reach and the result?
quiz.explanation: From indices 0–3 the farthest you can get is index 3 (0+3, 1+2, 2+1, 3+0). At i = 4, i > reach = 3, so the last index is unreachable.

quiz.question: Gas Station: if the total gas is at least the total cost, then…
options: A valid starting station is guaranteed to exist
Station 0 is always a valid start
Every station is a valid start
You still have to simulate from every station to know
quiz.explanation: Starting right after the lowest point of the running sum of gas − cost keeps the tank non-negative all the way round. That is why the one-pass algorithm can return its last candidate without re-checking.

quiz.question: Gas Station: starting at s, the tank first goes negative at station i. Why can every start between s and i be skipped?
options: The tank never goes negative again after a reset
Any start k in (s, i] reaches i with no more fuel than starting at s did, so it also runs out
We must start at the station with the most gas
quiz.explanation: The stretch s..k−1 had a non-negative running sum (the tank had not dropped below 0 yet). Starting at k throws that fuel away, so you arrive at i with the same or less — and still fail.

quiz.question: Partition Labels: what does "abacbddefe" return?
quiz.explanation: "abacb" must reach the last b (index 4), "dd" closes at 6, "efe" closes at 9 → sizes 5, 2, 3.

quiz.question: Insert Interval when the input is already sorted and non-overlapping — best time complexity?
quiz.explanation: One pass with three phases (before, overlapping, after). Re-sorting would cost O(n log n) for no reason; binary search can find the position in O(log n) but building the output is still O(n).

quiz.question: Which problem is NOT solved correctly by a greedy algorithm?
quiz.explanation: In 0/1 knapsack you cannot split items, so taking the best value/weight ratio first can waste capacity (weights [1,3,4,5], values [1,4,5,7], capacity 7: greedy 8, optimal 9). It needs DP; the other three have greedy proofs.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: [1,4] and [4,5] touch and merge (≤) into [1,5]; [6,8] and [7,9] overlap into [6,9]. Two blocks remain. With < instead of ≤ the answer would be 3.
